title: Collective Ring Formation in Active Matter
abstract: We study the formation of ring-like structures in interacting active particle systems in two dimensions. The emergent structure shows signatures of both spatial and orientational organization. The spatial organization is characterized by the radial distance of a tagged particle from the centroid of the assembly, while orientational organization is characterized by the radial alignment of its self-propulsion direction. We derive exact analytical expressions for the radial and polarization distributions for systems of active Brownian particles and run-and-tumble particles. While both models exhibit annular steady states, we show that their spatial and orientational organization differ qualitatively in the strongly active regime. A direct comparison of the two models reveals how the nature of the propulsion mechanism leads to the distinction in both the structure of the annulus and the statistics of particle orientations. Our results provide a unified analytical framework for characterizing emergent annular states in active matter and identify robust signatures that distinguish persistent active dynamics with continuous and discrete reorientation.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates how different propulsion mechanisms (ABP vs. RTP) affect the collective ring formation in active matter. By deriving exact analytical expressions, the authors show that while both types of particles form stable rings, the underlying physics dictates distinct spatial and orientational structures. This work provides a general framework for characterizing emergent non-equilibrium states.
main_problem: The study characterizes the difference in spatial and orientational organization between active particle systems with distinct propulsion mechanisms (Active Brownian Particles vs. Run-and-Tumble Particles).
main_result: Both models form stationary ring-like structures, but their spatial and orientational organizations differ qualitatively, providing a unified analytical framework to distinguish continuous versus discrete reorientation dynamics.
method: The analysis uses an analytical approach involving Langevin equations, characteristic functions, and expansions in the activity strength parameter ($\alpha$) to derive stationary distributions for radial position and polarization.
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ overdamped active particles interacting via a harmonic potential in two dimensions. The dynamics are modeled using self-propulsion terms for Active Brownian Particles (ABP) with continuous rotation, and Run-and-Tumble Particles (RTP) with discrete reorientation.
key_observables: Radial distance distribution $P(\ell)$ from the centroid, and radial polarization $\psi = \hat{\ell} \cdot \hat{n}$ (alignment between position and self-propulsion direction).
important_parameters: Activity strength parameter $\alpha = 1/(\mu	au)$, which distinguishes between strongly active ($\alpha \ll 1$) and passive ($\alpha \gg 1$) regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the large number of particles limit ($N \gg 1$) and approximations such as treating the relative motion noise as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate typical ring configurations comparing RTPs and ABPs, and show $P(\ell)$ for both models across varying activity parameters ($\alpha$), demonstrating structural differences in the annulus formation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and observables, derives analytical expressions for stationary distributions using characteristic functions (Appendix A), details the computation of $P(\ell)$ separately for RTPs (Appendix B) and ABPs (Appendix C), and concludes by comparing the resulting spatial and orientational signatures.
why_interesting: While focused on active matter rather than quantum systems, the rigorous analytical framework developed for non-equilibrium steady states in interacting particle systems provides powerful mathematical tools applicable to open quantum systems or many-body dynamics far from equilibrium.
